newsitem.title: FRANCE: Jospin committed to euro, deficit danger lingers.
newsitem.headline: Jospin committed to euro, deficit danger lingers.

text.p: French Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin said on Thursday his new left-wing government was committed to launching a single euro currency on time, but vowed to keep fighting for more solidarity, growth and jobs in Europe.

Jospin, delivering his maiden speech to parliament, made no mention of meeting the economic fitness criteria for European monetary union and said the euro currency must go hand in hand with economic solidarity to create growth and jobs.

Economists said he had little choice but to steer clear of declarations about France's public deficits and ability to pass the single currency test pending the outcome of an audit of state finances due in mid-July.

Some, however, said the underlying message was that public spending would rise and this could worsen already suspect finances with the risk of a public deficit overrun on a level that would be hard to sell to Germany.

"The feebleness of growth is a problem facing the whole of Europe. There must therefore be a common response. In this perspective, we reaffirm our determination to achieve economic and monetary union at the deadline provided for by the treaty," Jospin said in his keynote policy speech.

"But you cannot share a currency without creating economic solidarity. Concerning the independence of a (European) central bank, it does not mean a political vacuum. That was the meaning of the proposals we made (at this week's European Union summit) in Amsterdam," he said.

Jospin said the EU summit resolution on jobs and growth was only a start and France would push for a reinforcement of a social Europe. At home, he pledged to create the conditions for more vigorous economic growth.

While some economists saw his speech as an encouraging reaffirmation of the government's promise to sign up to a single currency, others said spending pledges were a threat to the project because they risked doing more damage to a deficit which would already have overshot the Maastricht treaty goals.

France could plead a case for a flexible reading of the Maastricht treaty goal of limiting public deficits to three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) but would find it hard to do so if the deficit was well over that amount, they said.
Germany, which has always argued vehemently for a strict interpretation of the deficit target even if it appears to have problems of its own, would find it very hard to swallow.
"If France is above 3.5 percent it'll be very hard to sell to Germany and the German people," said Eric Chaney, economist at Morgan Stanley bank in Paris.

He said promises by Jospin to quadruple special "return to school" payouts to families with children in education could add another 10 billion francs to spending and the government did not seem worried about closing a shortfall in tax income.
Chaney said he had been predicting a public deficit of 3.3 percent of GDP but that he now saw the risk of it hitting 3.5 or 3.6 percent.
Philippe Brossard at ABN Amro bank also saw the danger of tensions with Germany, while highlighting that Germany itself looked like it would have trouble sticking to the strict three percent.
"The Germans are going to start screaming that they're not doing the right thing and that they should be trying to get to three percent," he said.
"But in Germany the situation is hard as well, I don't see any way of them getting to three percent."
